Service Your Bike Before You Tour

Breaking down on a remote Highland road is every tourer's nightmare. The simplest way to avoid mechanical failure on tour is thorough pre-trip maintenance. A well-serviced motorcycle is a reliable motorcycle, and the peace of mind from knowing everything is in top condition lets you focus on enjoying the ride rather than worrying about the machinery.

Pre-Tour Service Checklist

  • Engine oil and filter — Fresh oil is cheap insurance. If your next oil change would fall during the tour, do it before you leave. Use the manufacturer-specified grade and a genuine or quality aftermarket filter.
  • Coolant — Check the level and condition. If it looks rusty or has not been changed in two years, flush and replace it. Coolant failure on a hot day can cause catastrophic engine damage.
  • Brake fluid — Brake fluid absorbs moisture over time, lowering its boiling point and reducing braking effectiveness. Replace every two years or if the fluid appears dark rather than clear amber.
  • Brake pads — Check thickness on all calipers. If pads will reach minimum thickness during the tour, replace them now. Carrying spare pads is wise for extended tours.
  • Chain and sprockets — Check chain tension, lubrication, and wear. Inspect sprocket teeth for hooking or wear. A chain that might last another 2,000 miles of commuting could fail under the sustained load of touring.
  • Tyres — Check tread depth, condition, and age. Fit fresh tyres if any doubt exists. Run them in for 100 miles before the tour to scrub off the release agent.
  • Lights — Check all bulbs, indicators, brake light, and horn. Replace any dim or flickering bulbs. Carry spares for non-LED lights.

Additional Checks for Long Tours

Wheel bearings: Grab each wheel and try to rock it side to side. Any play indicates worn bearings that need replacement. Bearing failure on tour causes catastrophic wheel wobble.

Suspension linkages: Check for play in swingarm and linkage bearings. Lubricate pivot points if they have grease nipples.

Battery: Check terminal connections are tight and clean. Load-test the battery if it is over three years old. A failing battery will strand you when the bike refuses to start at a remote fuel stop.

Book your pre-tour service at least two weeks before departure. This gives time for any parts to be ordered and fitted, and for you to ride the bike and confirm everything feels correct before loading up for the tour.

During-Tour Maintenance

On tour, check tyre pressures every morning, lubricate the chain every 300-500 miles, and do a visual inspection of lights, brake pads, and fluid levels at each fuel stop. keyTakeaways: Thorough pre-trip maintenance is the simplest way to avoid a remote breakdown.
Change oil and filter before you leave if a service would fall during the tour.
Replace brake fluid every two years as it absorbs moisture and loses effectiveness.
Fit fresh tyres if in doubt and run them in for 100 miles before the tour.
Book your pre-tour service at least two weeks before departure.

pros: Peace of mind lets you focus on the ride, not the machinery.
Catches worn consumables before they fail far from home.
Cheap insurance against expensive roadside drama.
cons: Requires booking and budgeting time before departure.
Parts for major items may need ordering in advance.

faq.q: How far ahead should I service before a tour?
faq.a: Book your pre-tour service at least two weeks before departure. This gives time for any parts to be ordered and fitted, and lets you ride the bike to confirm everything feels correct before loading up. Leaving it to the last minute risks travelling on unproven work.

faq.q: How often should brake fluid be changed?
faq.a: Replace brake fluid every two years, or sooner if it appears dark rather than clear amber. Brake fluid absorbs moisture over time, which lowers its boiling point and reduces braking effectiveness, a real risk on long descents in the Highlands or Lake District when carrying luggage.

faq.q: What should I check for long or remote tours?
faq.a: Beyond the basic service, rock each wheel to check for bearing play, inspect swingarm and linkage bearings, and load-test a battery over three years old. Wheel bearing or battery failure can strand you 50 miles from the nearest village with no phone signal, so these checks are worthwhile.

faq.q: What maintenance should I do during the tour?
faq.a: Check tyre pressures every morning, lubricate the chain every 300-500 miles, and do a visual inspection of lights, brake pads and fluid levels at each fuel stop. Five minutes of daily checks prevents hours of roadside drama and catches small issues before they become failures.
